technical_projects.STANDOUT_DETAIL: The tool is deployed on **helpingminds.ca — Justin's own non-profit's domain** — not on a generic free-tier host. This is materially stronger than a GitHub repo alone because it closes the narrative loop completely and verifiably: a grade-9 classmate's mental-health crisis → he founds HelpingMinds.ca → he teaches himself LightGBM/XGBoost → he builds a screening tool → he deploys it on his own organisation where students can actually reach it. A supplementary application reader can click one link and see the whole arc is real. Very few applicants can produce that.
technical_projects.ethics_and_safety_assessment: VERIFIED 2026-08-03 AND HE GOT THIS RIGHT — worth saying explicitly, because handled badly this would have been a liability rather than an asset. A publicly accessible mental-health screening tool aimed at minors is exactly the kind of project that alarms a health-sciences reviewer if the safeguards are missing. Justin's implementation has all of them: (1) CLIENT-SIDE ONLY — the page states twice that 'your answers never leave your browser. No data is collected, stored, or sent anywhere,' which pre-empts the single biggest objection; (2) explicit NON-DIAGNOSTIC disclaimer — 'a screening tool, not a medical diagnosis... should not replace professional evaluation'; (3) CRISIS RESOURCES prominently displayed on both the tool and the README — Kids Help Phone 1-800-668-6868, Crisis Text Line (text HELLO to 686868), and 9-8-8; (4) the survey asks a suicidal-ideation question and pairs it with those crisis lines, which is the responsible way to ask it; (5) proper ATTRIBUTION of the Kaggle dataset and its original creator. This should be mentioned in supplementary applications — the judgement shown here is itself the credential.

gaps_and_next_steps.1_no_performance_metrics: The README reports no accuracy, AUC, precision/recall, confusion matrix or calibration. For a screening tool this is the most conspicuous absence — any technical reader, and any BHSc reviewer who thinks about it for ten seconds, will ask 'how good is it?' and find no answer. He has these numbers from training. Easiest high-value fix available; roughly an hour.
gaps_and_next_steps.2_population_mismatch_IS_THE_GOLD: The model is trained on a Kaggle competition dataset and deployed for Canadian high-school students aged 14-19. Those are not the same population, and the README's limitations text does not name it. This is NOT a flaw to hide — it is the single best supplementary-application material in the entire profile, and it is the same move that made the Harvard answer strong: 'the Roboflow model was trained on 200 images under different lighting and failed in the live demo.' Here the equivalent is: 'I trained on a dataset whose population differs from the students I built this for, and deployed it anyway as a screening aid rather than a diagnostic — here is why that matters, and here is what would fix it: validation against real local student data.' That is a 7/7 answer, and it connects directly to the research-validation pitch he was already advised to make to UofA researchers. ALSO CONFIRM: Kaggle Playground Series datasets are generally described on the competition page as synthetically generated from an original dataset. Justin should check the S4E11 competition page and, if so, state that provenance explicitly — training a deployed tool on synthetic data is a real and interesting limitation to own.
gaps_and_next_steps.3_linkedin_writeup: The remaining A3 piece. Build it around gap 2, not around a feature list. One specific finding that surprised him plus the honest population-mismatch problem, in the style of his Titanic retrospective. This is also the artifact that makes the repo and tool discoverable to anyone who is not already looking for them.

caveats.label: Self-selection bias
caveats.body: Reddit users overwhelmingly post when they're accepted (~93-99% of decisions reported are acceptances). Treat all 'accepted average' numbers as the FLOOR of what gets in, not as a 50/50 cutoff line. Justin's percentile is relative to admitted students, not raw applicant pools.

caveats.label: OOP small samples
caveats.body: Out-of-province sample sizes are 4-12 reports per program. The verdict model treats OOP floors as directional only when n_oop < 10 — small-sample minimums are too noisy to override percentile-based verdicts.

caveats.label: McMaster BHSc OOP yellow flag
caveats.body: Only 5 OOP-accepted reports for McMaster BHSc across 4 cycles, all with averages ≥ 97.8%. The verdict model surfaces this as directional rather than verdict-changing, but it suggests the OOP bar may be meaningfully higher than in-province. Justin should know this.

caveats.label: Schema drift across cycles
caveats.body: The 4 Reddit forms used different question sets across years. The normalizer maps everything to a canonical 'best_avg' field. See workflows/clean_application_data.md for details.

caveats.label: 2025-26 cycle still in progress
caveats.body: The 2025-2026 cycles (Ontario + Alberta) are still receiving submissions through ~end of May 2026. Numbers from that cycle are provisional and skew toward earlier-cycle decisions.

caveats.label: Tier-2 requirements confidence: medium
caveats.body: All 9 Tier-2 requirement entries are confidence=medium. Prerequisite courses are high-confidence (well-known and stable); specific dates default to the universal Jan 15 OUAC date and competitive averages are educated guesses anchored to Reddit data.

caveats.label: Tier-3/4 not curated
caveats.body: Tier-3 (Waterloo CS variants) and Tier-4 (UAlberta) program requirements have NOT been curated. Their checklist rows are blank.

caveats.label: Dates are shifted +1 year from cycle template
caveats.body: Curated requirements use the 2025-2026 cycle as a template. The dashboard shifts every date by +365 days to reflect Justin's actual application cycle (2026-2027). OUAC and supp deadlines may shift by ±1 day in the actual cycle — verify against official sources before relying on exact dates.
